speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry what is the strategy for growing our economy and creating good jobs for Singaporeans without an over-reliance on foreign manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Quality jobs provide good wages; and good wages and opportunities enable Singaporeans to pursue our dreams.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The competition for quality investments has never been easy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Without natural resources, we strive hard to create our own competitive advantages and build up a strong reputation and trusted brand name for Singapore based on the following: political stability, rule of law, a progressive business environment, cohesive tripartite relations, skilled workers, physical and non-physical connectivity of air, land, sea, data, finance, talent, technologies and regulations, intellectual property protection and consistency of policy execution over the long term.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: However, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, beyond all the above factors, the size and quality of our talent pool still matters.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Too small a talent pool and our enterprises will find it hard to compete with the big global players; an inability to scale or transcend our geographical size and location will hinder our overall competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The quality of our talent pool is equally important.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It allows us to overcome the limitations of size to attract high-quality and high value-add investments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Talent is thus critical to ensure that we are able to win the quality investments not only for this generation but also for future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: On the other hand, the loss of a quality investment means more than the loss of competitiveness and good job opportunities for this generation of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The red Lego bricks we see in Figure 1 represents the Singapore workforce.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we only have the Singaporean workforce, the size of our economy will only be so big and the wages of our people only so high, as shown in Figure 1.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The foreign complement is the one in yellow.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, even at this stage, there will still be many Singaporeans with the talent and aspirations to achieve even better prospects and higher wages, either in Singapore or elsewhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To achieve that, we need higher quality investments that can create even higher paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This will often require us to bring in some foreign workers at different skills levels to complement the local workforce to win the next slate of high-quality investments that can provide more high-paying jobs for Singaporeans, as shown in Figure 3.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Otherwise, our globally mobile and competitive Singaporeans will leave for greener pastures elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We may ask, "Why do we not have all the Singaporeans doing the highest paying jobs immediately?" This was where I left off in the last Parliament session where I explained the dilemma and the trade-offs, and asked if we would take a new investment that provides many good jobs for Singaporeans, but some of the higher paying jobs in the company are initially filled by foreigners, as shown in the diagram in Figure 3.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the first step, we did not have all the Singaporeans taking all the highest paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Do we want such an investment in Singapore or should we turn it down and let the company invest in another country?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we turn it down, we immediately lose the large number of good jobs that Singaporeans can have, brought about by this investment.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We also lose the opportunity for Singaporeans to take on higher level positions over time, as these jobs are no longer in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our strategy is to win the investment first not just for this generation, but for the next.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Work hard to quickly upgrade the skills of our workers to take on these higher paying jobs as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Progressively, our workers will have opportunities to take on those jobs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And, certainly, the next generation who are better educated, will have better opportunities as shown in Figure 4.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Over time, more and more of the lower-wage and lower-productivity jobs will be moved out of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Within Singapore, these jobs will be increasingly filled by foreign workers as companies are unable to attract enough Singaporeans to take on these positions, as shown in Figure 5.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is not the end of the story.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Every generation, with a combination of a local and foreign workforce working together to win the next better investment for this generation and the rest.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Every generation, working hard to upgrade the skills to take on the higher-skilled jobs progressively, earning higher pay in the process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And throughout the process, making sure that the red bricks that represent the Singapore Core remain the foundational pillars of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This was the story of electronics to semiconductors that I shared in Parliament in the last Sitting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, Esther Ng and Alice Low – two ladies – went from being operators in Texas Instruments in 1969 to become a document control assistant and a technician in the yield enhancement lab of Micron respectively, earning higher wages than when they first started.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They have since retired and they have both contributed to developing the industry for future generations to benefit from.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our local businesses have also benefited from attracting high-quality investments.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: A local small and medium enterprise (SME), CK Shipping, went from a traditional logistics player to be a specialised aerospace logistics provider for Singapore Aero Engine Services Private Limited (SAESL), a joint venture between Rolls Royce and SIA Engineering.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: CK Shipping also worked with Enterprise Singapore to reskill their workers to build capabilities in the new sector, allowing Singaporean workers to benefit from the new opportunities created.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Esther, Alice and CK Shipping would not have risen in their stations had we not attracted new investments and progressively upgraded our economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What was true for the electronics to semiconductor story and shipping is true for all sectors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, we are seeing the same story unfolding before us in the data, digitalisation and ICT sectors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is what we are doing – to grow new sectors like Advanced Manufacturing, Agri-tech and to transform our existing sectors like logistics and hospitality.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our fresh graduates from universities and polytechnics are progressively filling up these higher-skilled, higher-paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we will step up our mid-career upgrading programmes for our middle-age workers to keep pace with these new technologies and new industries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we need a balanced approach to our talent strategy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Too few, our local enterprises and workers are unable to achieve scale or competitiveness for the global market.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Hence, it is a strategy that requires constant finetuning to get the balance right for enterprises and workers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Beyond quantity and quality, we must also diversify our foreign manpower sources and there are good reasons for this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: From a business continuity perspective, we must manage the risk of overly relying on any particular source for any particular type of foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: From a social perspective, we must manage the externalities associated with too high a concentration of any particular foreign labour source.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Singapore is a diverse, cosmopolitan and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we must also not ignore the public discomfort that can surface with too high a concentration of any particular foreign worker group.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Again, this is a work in constant finetuning, based on the acceptance of foreigners by our society and the manpower needs of our companies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To grow our economy and job opportunities, we will always need a certain local-foreign complement, both in terms of quality and quantity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, we must manage the number and quality of the foreign complement to strike a good balance between economic needs and social acceptance.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Last but not least, progressively enable more and more Singaporeans to take on the higher-paying jobs from our investments.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This was how we transformed from Third World to First and this was how we secured and will secure a brighter future and better lives for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, if I recall, I believe the Workers' Party also raised this possibility previously.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I do not know if the Workers' Party still advocates this, but I remember hearing this as well, sometime back in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Pritam Singh can correct me if I am wrong.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we are able to attract an investment that comes in and creates two new jobs at $7,000 and $10,000.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But bearing in mind that, essentially in Singapore, we are almost at full employment and our labour force participation rate is already one of the highest in the world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Which means that cumulatively, we have very little spare capacity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Singaporean is now holding the $5,000 job.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have the prospect of having two new jobs at $7,000, $10,000, with a new investment.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Supposing, as a thought process, we say that we will not allow any fresh foreign worker to come in.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The only way that we can bring in that investment is: first, there must be two Singaporeans available to do those jobs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, the chances are that if we do not have circulation space for our manpower, chances are that we will forgo that investment, because we have essentially full employment, one of the world's highest labour force participation rate, but we have no spare capacity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we cannot free up two in time to take the new investment.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we will lose the investment for this generation and the next.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There is another possible scenario, which is that we also keep to the 0% foreign workforce growth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What it means is that we give ourselves a small discount that, in the short term, we allow a surge of a foreign workforce complement to come in.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we shift the Singaporean over to the new jobs – the $7,000 and $10,000 jobs, if possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Then, we have to ask ourselves what do we do for the two jobs that are being vacated in the $5,000 job company?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we have zero-foreign workforce growth, that means that the company with the $5,000 job will not get a foreign substitute in place of the two Singaporeans that have left, which means that that company will likely be unsustainable, which means that the rest of the Singaporeans in that company will also likely be displaced once that company becomes not viable.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: While it is theoretically possible, there is a third possibility, which is we will tell everyone to improve their productivity as much as they can to release the two workers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Retrain them and then we can take on the new investment and we do not need new foreign workforce.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we also know that in the real world, it is not easy to do because different industries will have different opportunities for productivity growth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Manufacturing will be much higher than services, for example.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And the speed and skill at which we can retrain and upskill our workers are dependent on many factors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Whether we can do it in time to catch the new investment is always uncertain.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, the foreign workforce growth is one way to overcome this circulation for the companies to transit, just as the model I showed during the slideshow just now.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Over time, some of the lower value-add and lower productivity jobs will have to be displaced, in order for us to take on the higher value-add, higher productivity jobs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But it takes a process and it takes circulation space, which is why while we maintain the overall growth trajectory over a period of time, we must be careful not to crash the gears and make our enterprises suffer the consequences of the lack of capacity to circulate and regenerate capacity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We must also be cognisant of the ability and the pace which we can reskill and upgrade our workers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, while it is a theoretical possibility, we should not take it lightly and assume that there are no serious implications with a crashing of gears.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we are obviously cognisant that foreign workforce growth cannot grow indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Over time, there must be circulation, where the higher-quality ones displace the lower-quality ones, and that is how, progressively, generation by generation, we created space.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we refer back to the model that I used.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If from Figure 1 to Figure 5, and the total number of Singaporeans is still the same, and everything is foreign complement, then the balance would be totally lopsided.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But over time, you would notice that by the time we reach Figure 5, the bottom part is hollowed out; and that is how we maintain the overall stance.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will conclude by sharing one other aspect with this House.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is a tremendous challenge for the enterprises to make the necessary adjustments.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will have to ask ourselves how do we get to that stage and emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Everything that we do now must prepare for the day where our local labour force peaks, because the choices are stark.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we maintain the current ratio of local-foreign, when local workforce peaks, foreign workforce must peak.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When local workforce falls, foreign workforce must fall, and the total must fall.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The position then was keeping the foreign workforce numbers constant, as the Minister shared, but if a 1% resident workforce growth target was achieved, there was a caveat to that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, that is just as a matter of clarification, notwithstanding the Minister's reasoning as to how difficult that balancing act will be and the situation as the numbers peak in this decade.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There was another point that came out of that debate, if I remember, and I do apologise if I get my facts wrong here, but I do believe that the entire population policy and the way we are moving forward would be up for review at the end of the decade.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Those were the terms – end of the decade.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My question really is are we going to have a debate, a Motion on this matter, on the population issue, very much because the Minister raises an important point about how significant the upcoming decade will be for overall strategy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think for Question and Answer time, the Standing Orders do say that it should not be a pretext for a debate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That is the word in the Standing Orders, but I think we probably need a longer and more extensive discussion in Parliament about this matter.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Is Mr Pritam Singh asking me for a ruling on his third question?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is just we have had episodes where Question and Answer time goes on to a pretty substantive issue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I think we, perhaps, should deal with it in another way.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, zero foreign workforce growth, if 1% resident growth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Given our TFR, it is not a given that we will be anywhere near this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the other hand, to what extent can we bring in fresh immigrants to supplement?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, today, if I may be frank, even if we try, whether Singapore can be the choice location for other people is an open question.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I always jokingly say immigration is the story of unrequited love.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Those whom we want may not want us, and those whom we do not want, may all want to come.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is not easy because there is the other dimension, which perhaps the Member did not say in his clarification.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Let us take the current moment; the current moment with the virus outbreak.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There would be a significant impact on our economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Whether we can still maintain that trajectory that we are shooting for is not a given.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We cannot assume that economic growth will keep going at the rate that we desire.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We aim for the best but we may not always get it.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why even in the previous population debate, to grow very fast sometimes has its challenges, but to grow not sufficiently fast, is also a challenge.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we do not grow sufficiently fast, the opportunities are not there for our next generation, it is a challenge.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we do not grow sufficiently fast and people bypass us and we lose our strategic relevance, it is also a challenge.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But can I ask him to recall and to confirm if this was also raised in the General Election (GE) 2015 Workers' Party's manifesto, the same proposal about curbing and having zero-foreign workforce growth?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Is that a proposal that is also in the GE 2015 Workers' Party's manifesto?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second, if I hear Mr Pritam Singh correctly, he said he had a caveat.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If I heard him correctly, I think he is saying that he does support that we do need a local-foreign workforce complement.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I just wanted to seek those two points of clarification from Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Pritam Singh, you can answer but I would take the point that you made earlier that Questions for Oral Answers are meant for backbenchers to ask the front bench questions about Government policies.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, perhaps, you may want to keep your answer to the point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Deputy Speaker, you have put me in a bit of a bind here.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The first reply, I do not have that information offhand, I will have to check the facts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I believe the Senior Minister of State is not one just to speak without having the facts at the back of his hand, so he must have the manifesto in front of him.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second question was about supporting the balance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This is something we have to look at very carefully.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: All the time we ask for data, it is not data for the sake of data.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think it is to understand the Government's perspective because it is not a case of throwing whatever the Government is saying out of the window or turning up our noses at it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But, certainly, we have to look at it very carefully.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If the Government makes a compelling case, then there is no reason for us to be objectionable about it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But it is, certainly, something we have to look at.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And that is why my initial question was about when are we reviewing the overall population plan, which was discussed in 2013 that the timeline is at the end of the decade when we will review where we are going and what the future is going to look like.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, we will be in a better position to answer the questions and provide another perspective to the Government's plans at that point.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: All right, we will move on from here.
